# v1.1.0-dev.59 — Display zoom and resolution

Pre-release off the `dev` branch. Builds on `v1.1.0-dev.58`.

dev.58 shipped the design for this. This one ships the feature.

A profile can now set your display scaling — the percentage in
Settings → System → Display that everyone calls zoom — and your
resolution, before it puts your windows back. And you can pair a
zoom level with a resolution so that setting one sets the other.

## The Display Button

Select a profile and you'll see a new **Display** pill next to
Hotkey and Hold. It opens an editor with two halves.

**Monitors.** Every connected display gets a scaling dropdown and
a resolution dropdown, both filled from what Windows actually
reports for that monitor — no guessing, no hardcoded lists. Leave
either on "Leave unchanged" and the profile won't touch it. Each
row shows what the monitor is set to right now, so you can see
what you're changing from.

The scaling dropdown also offers **Step up one** and **Step down
one**. Those are relative: they move one rung along whatever
ladder that monitor supports, resolved at the moment you press
the key rather than baked in when you saved. That's what you want
on a hotkey.

**Zoom → resolution mapping.** Pair a percentage with a
resolution for a specific monitor — say 150% with 2560×1440.
From then on, whenever that monitor gets set to 150%, the
resolution comes with it. By this profile, by a step hotkey, by
any other preset. The mapping is stored per monitor rather than
per profile, because it describes the hardware: if 150% means
2560×1440 on your 4K panel, that's true no matter which layout
you're loading.

## Zoom Presets

Tick **Display-only preset** and the profile stops being a window
layout and becomes purely a display preset. No windows saved, no
windows moved — it just applies the scaling and resolution.

Because it's still a profile, it picks up everything profiles
already have. Give it a hotkey through the same capture dialog.
It shows up in the tray menu, the Jump List, the command palette,
`--load=`, and `wlm://` links. Nothing new to learn.

Display-only presets are deliberately kept out of auto-activation,
so binding one to a monitor set can't make it beat the actual
layout profile you wanted.

## Turning It On

This is **off by default**, in Settings → Auto-activation →
Display configuration. Nothing that already exists on your machine
starts changing your display after you update. Flip the checkbox
when you want it.

## About The Windows Side Of This

Changing resolution is a documented, stable Windows API and has
been since the nineties.

Changing the **scaling percentage** is not. Windows exposes no
supported way to do it. The Settings app uses an internal call
that was worked out by reading `user32.dll`, and that's what this
uses too. Microsoft could change or remove it in any update.

So it sits behind a capability check. If your build stops
accepting it, the editor disables the scaling controls and tells
you why, in those words, and the resolution half carries on
working. What it will not do is quietly fail and let you think it
worked.

The same principle runs through the rest of it. Ask for a
percentage your monitor can't do and you're told it was clamped
and to what — not handed a success message. Ask for a resolution
your driver doesn't offer and you're told that too. After every
change the app re-reads the display and checks the value actually
landed, because there is a known Windows 11 24H2 bug where a
resolution change against a virtual display reports success while
nothing happens. If that bites, you get told.

## If You Use A Virtual Display

Parsec's virtual adapter, and some others, report a scaling range
that disagrees with what Windows is really doing — claiming only
100% is available while the desktop sits at 200%. Where that
happens the editor shows you both numbers and says the control
may not behave, instead of printing a figure it knows is
contradicted. Resolution is unaffected.

## While We Were In There

Three long-standing problems with the profile schema got fixed.
`$schema` and `knownMonitorSets` were being written into every
profile but weren't declared as allowed fields, which meant every
profile WLM has ever saved failed validation against its own
schema. If you hand-edit profiles in an editor, the squiggly
underlines should be gone.

## Install

Auto-updates from dev.53 and later. Otherwise unzip and run.
